analysis.one_liner: Bans preexisting-condition exclusions, strips health insurers' antitrust exemption, lets Medicare negotiate drug prices, and allows cheaper drug importation.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to five House committees in March 2010, was never taken up or voted on, and expired when the 111th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill was a slimmed-down health reform package introduced during the Affordable Care Act debate. It would bar insurers from denying or pricing coverage based on a person's health history, require them to accept every applicant, and strip their long-standing exemption from federal antitrust laws. It would also let Medicare run its own prescription drug plan and negotiate prices directly with manufacturers, allow importation of cheaper drugs from Canada and other approved countries, and end higher Medicare Advantage payments.
analysis.who_benefits: People with preexisting conditions who could be denied coverage; policyholders whose premiums are spent on administration rather than care; Medicare beneficiaries paying high drug prices; and independent pharmacies squeezed by reimbursement rules.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People with preexisting conditions and Medicare drug users

how_it_helps.text: Bans insurers from imposing preexisting-condition exclusions or varying premiums based on health status, medical history, genetic information, disability, or source of injury.
Requires every insurer offering coverage in a state to accept every employer and individual who applies, guarantees renewal, and prohibits canceling (rescinding) policies except in cases of fraud.
Amends the McCarran-Ferguson Act so federal antitrust laws again apply to insurers' price fixing, market allocation, and monopolization, ending the industry's exemption.
Requires group-market insurers to rebate premiums to enrollees whenever their medical loss ratio falls below 92 percent, meaning at least 92 cents of every premium dollar goes to medical care.

Creates a Medicare-operated prescription drug plan under which the HHS Secretary negotiates drug prices directly with pharmaceutical manufacturers, using a formulary built on clinical evidence and value.

Waives import restrictions so registered pharmacies, wholesalers, and individuals can import qualifying prescription drugs from Canada and other countries the Secretary certifies as having equivalent safety standards, with chain-of-custody and anti-counterfeiting safeguards.

Phases Medicare Advantage payments down to a blended benchmark tied to local fee-for-service costs and eliminates the Medicare Advantage Regional Plan Stabilization Fund, reducing overpayments to private plans.
Disallows the income tax deduction for advertising and promotional expenses for prescription pharmaceuticals, ending a public subsidy for direct-to-consumer drug ads.
Requires pharmacy benefit managers with health plan contracts to comply with fiduciary standards set by HHS.

Raises Medicaid pharmacy reimbursement floors and redefines average manufacturer price in ways favorable to retail community pharmacies, and exempts pharmacies from certain Medicare accreditation requirements.

Sets a floor of 1.00 on the Medicare hospital area wage index and the physician practice-expense geographic index, reducing payment disparities that shortchange rural and lower-wage-area hospitals and doctors.

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers and Medicare Advantage plans give up antitrust protection, guaranteed-issue obligations, and higher payment benchmarks. Brand-name drug makers lose Medicare negotiation, face import competition, and lose the advertising deduction. Pharmacy benefit managers face fiduciary rules. The Treasury loses a modest amount from the advertising deduction change, and administrative costs of the importation system are paid through fees on registered importers and exporters.
analysis.who_pays_short: Health insurers, Medicare Advantage plans, and drug makers

drawbacks.text: The bill sharply limits federal abortion funding to cases where a physical condition endangers the woman's life, rape, or incest, narrower than some existing exceptions, and requires any abortion coverage to be purchased separately with non-federal funds.
Prohibits insurers from selling coverage to anyone who is not a citizen or lawfully present, even if the person pays the premiums entirely with their own money.

The bill requires insurers to accept all applicants but includes no requirement that individuals carry coverage, which could concentrate sicker, costlier people in the insurance pool and push premiums up for everyone else.
A flat 92 percent medical loss ratio on all group plans is stricter than the thresholds later enacted in federal law, which could push some insurers out of smaller or less profitable markets.

Opening commercial drug importation creates regulatory and safety costs; the bill addresses them with registration, inspections, bonds, and track-and-trace requirements, but oversight of foreign supply chains would be a real ongoing burden for FDA and Customs.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core consumer protections — guaranteed issue, an end to preexisting-condition denials and health-based pricing, antitrust exposure, and Medicare drug negotiation — are substantial and directly targeted at practices that raise costs or deny care. The main honest objections are design ones: guaranteeing coverage without a coverage mandate risks adverse-selection premium spirals, and the 92 percent loss-ratio floor is aggressive. The abortion-funding and lawful-resident restrictions narrow who benefits. On balance the bill is clearly weighted toward patients and taxpayers, though it is a partial package rather than the comprehensive restructuring of the ACA it competed against.

outcome.mechanism: The bill went to five House committees and their subcommittees in March and April 2010, none of which ever held a markup or vote on it, and it died when the 111th Congress ended in January 2011.

narrative.text: Rep. Marion Berry, a Democrat from Arkansas, introduced the bill on March 10, 2010, during the final weeks of the Affordable Care Act debate.
The same day, the House referred it to five committees: Energy and Commerce, plus the Judiciary, Oversight and Government Reform, Ways and Means, and Education and Labor committees.

The bill was then referred to three subcommittees — Health, Employment, Labor and Pensions; Courts and Competition Policy; and Immigration, Citizenship, Refugees, Border Security and International Law — in late March and April 2010.
No committee reported the bill, no markup or floor vote was ever held, and it received only two cosponsors before Congress ended.

The bill's provisions overlap with the Affordable Care Act enacted later in March 2010, which included guaranteed issue, a preexisting-condition ban, rating restrictions, medical loss ratio rebates, and Medicare Advantage payment cuts, but did not include insurer antitrust repeal, Medicare price negotiation, or drug importation.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers kept their antitrust exemption, Medicare Advantage plans kept higher benchmarks, and brand-name drug makers kept price-setting power, no importation, and the advertising deduction. Many of the bill's insurance-market rules were enacted weeks later through the Affordable Care Act, but its drug-price, antitrust, and PBM provisions never became law.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Health insurers and brand-name drug makers

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken, so the partisan shape was never tested; the sponsor was a Democrat, but the bill drew one Democratic and one Republican cosponsor.

industries.note: The bill strips the industry's McCarran-Ferguson antitrust exemption, requires guaranteed issue and renewability, bans health-based pricing and rescission, and mandates rebates when the medical loss ratio falls below 92 percent. Insurers profited from health-based underpricing of sick customers and from the exemption that allowed coordinated pricing; the bill removes both, which is why the industry's interest ran against patients here.

The bill phases payments down to a blended benchmark tied to local fee-for-service costs and eliminates the Regional Plan Stabilization Fund, cutting the extra payments private plans received over traditional Medicare, which were ultimately paid by taxpayers and beneficiaries.

A Medicare-operated drug plan would have the government negotiate prices directly with manufacturers, importation would expose U.S. prices to cheaper foreign markets, and the bill ends the tax deduction for direct-to-consumer drug advertising. Manufacturers' interest in maintaining U.S. price levels runs against patients paying those prices.

The bill imposes HHS fiduciary standards on PBMs and excludes payments involving PBMs from the average manufacturer price calculations that set Medicaid reimbursement. PBM interests in opaque pricing and spread capture ran against pharmacies and payers.

The bill raises Medicaid reimbursement floors, recalculates average manufacturer price to capture rebates routed through PBMs, and exempts pharmacies from certain Medicare accreditation requirements. Community pharmacies' higher reimbursement comes directly out of drug-maker margins, so their interest runs alongside patients' access to local drugstores.

industries.industry: Drug importers and foreign internet pharmacies
industries.note: The bill creates a legal, registered channel for personal and commercial importation from Canada and other approved countries, a market that is currently blocked. Consumers gain access to lower foreign prices, with the safeguards and fees built into the registration regime.
